items.title: Concept: what lives in memory and when the disk is touched
items.body:
While the app runs, the tasks live in a `List<Task>` inside `TaskManager`. The disk is a separate copy, and the two only meet at specific moments. Knowing those moments explains most surprises in a program like this.

Trace these yourself in the code:

- **Startup.** Follow `App.main` into `run()` and `loadTasksFromDisk`. What happens on the normal path, when the file is missing, and inside the `catch`?
- **Ids.** Find every line that assigns or changes `nextId`. For each one, note when it runs: at startup, on add, or on delete.
- **Shutdown.** Look at how `run()` is structured with `try` and `finally`. Which paths out of the loop reach the save, and what would happen if `scanner.nextLine()` threw?
- **The save itself.** Read the first line of `saveTasks` and look up what `Files.newBufferedWriter` does to an existing file by default.

Write your answers down, then test them by running the app with piped input.

items.title: Why typing -1 returns to the menu silently
items.body:
`readTaskId` uses `-1` as its "bad input" sentinel. When the user types `-1`, `Integer.parseInt` succeeds and returns -1, so the method returns the same value it would return for bad input, but without printing anything. `deleteTask` then checks `taskId == -1` and returns early, so the user sees the menu again with **no message at all**.

- *"Please enter a valid whole number."*: that line is printed only inside the `catch` for `NumberFormatException`, and -1 parses fine.
- *"Task not found."*: the manager is never called, because the early return happens first.
- *Deletes the last task*: ids are plain numbers matched with `==`; nothing counts from the end of the list.

items.title: Start here: four classes and the order to read them
items.body:
This is a terminal to-do list in plain Java 17: no frameworks, no database, one text file. Four classes each own one job:

1. **src/todo/model/Task.java** - one to-do item and its completion state.
2. **src/todo/service/TaskManager.java** - the in-memory list, ids, and the rules for add, complete and delete.
3. **src/todo/App.java** - the menu loop, reading input, and the moments the app touches the disk.
4. **src/todo/repository/TaskRepository.java** - turning the text file into Task objects and back.

Read them in that order (the README and docs/onboarding/01-reading-order.md explain why). The README describes every method; use it as a map, then confirm each claim in the code, because the questions in this quest are about what the code actually does.

The best way to check yourself is to run it. Compile with the javac line in the README, start it with `java -cp out todo.App`, and try odd input on purpose: an id that does not exist, the same action twice, a hand-edited data file.

excerpts.quote: The structure is small, but each class has one main responsibility:
understand the data 2. understand the rules 3. understand the program flow 4. understand persistence

The four reading stages and the tracing exercises to do after each one.

items.title: Why completed=yes loads as an open task
items.body:
`parseTask` converts the value with `Boolean.parseBoolean`, which returns true only for the text "true" (ignoring case) and returns false for anything else. It never throws. So `completed` becomes `false` (not null), the required-field check passes, and the task loads as **not completed** with no warning.

- *Loading fails*: only a missing field, a line without `=`, a bad number or a bad date makes the load fail; parseBoolean cannot.
- *Any non-empty value counts as true*: that is not how `Boolean.parseBoolean` works.
- *The block is skipped*: the parser never skips blocks; a block either loads or the whole load fails.

readMore.why: The persistence checklist names this silent-false behaviour as a subtle bug.

items.title: How one bad line erases the whole file
items.body:
Three pieces of code combine. `parseTask` throws an `IOException` for any line without `=`, so the line `garbage` fails the whole load. `loadTasksFromDisk` catches it, prints "Could not load tasks", and gives the manager an empty list. Then the `finally` block in `run()` calls `saveTasksToDisk`, and `Files.newBufferedWriter` truncates the file before writing the (empty) list. The file ends at **0 bytes**.

- *A failed load switches saving off*: there is no flag like that; the save in `finally` always runs.
- *The stray line is skipped*: one bad line aborts the whole load; nothing skips it.
- *saveTasks does not write an empty list*: it opens the writer first and simply loops zero times.

excerpts.quote: throw new IOException("Invalid line in data file: " + line);

items.title: Concept: the tasks.txt block format and its parser
items.body:
The app saves to a custom text format instead of JSON or CSV. Each task is a **block** of `key=value` lines, and a line holding only `---` ends the block. The README shows one complete block.

A hand-written parser like this has to make many small decisions, and each one changes what happens to a file that a person edited by hand or that another version wrote. Open `TaskRepository.parseTask` and `loadTasks` and answer these from the code:

- How is one line divided into a key and a value? Look at the exact `split` call and its second argument.
- Which keys must be present, and which may be missing or blank?
- What happens in the `switch` for a key that is not listed?
- How is text turned into a boolean, a number and a date, and which of those conversions can throw?
- Which exceptions are wrapped into an `IOException`, and who catches that?

Then compare with `saveTasks`: list the keys it writes. A format is only safe when the writer and the reader agree.

excerpts.quote: id=1 title=Buy milk description=From the grocery store
The project uses a simple custom text format instead of JSON or CSV.

Why this format was chosen, and the tradeoff against JSON.

items.title: Why a title containing = round-trips intact
items.body:
Saving writes the line `title=x=y`. On load, `parseTask` calls `line.split("=", 2)`. The limit 2 means "at most two parts", so the split happens at the first `=` only: the key is `title` and the value is `x=y`. The title comes back **unchanged** (reproduced with the title a=b).

- *Only x survives*: that would need a split without a limit followed by taking part 1; the limit keeps the rest of the line together.
- *Only y survives*: no code looks for the last `=`.
- *The block fails to parse*: a line is invalid only when it has no `=`, giving one part.

items.title: Why an unknown key survives loading but not saving
items.body:
The `switch` in `parseTask` handles six keys and has an empty `default` branch, so `priority=high` is read, matched to nothing and dropped. The line does contain `=`, so it is not an invalid line. When the app later saves, `saveTasks` writes exactly six fixed keys per task. The priority data is **ignored on load and gone after the next save**.

- *Loading fails*: the invalid-line error is only for a line with no `=` at all.
- *Kept and written back*: `Task` has no field for it and `saveTasks` writes only the fields it knows.
- *Appended to the description*: `description` is only set by the `description` case.

items.title: Why completing a task twice changes nothing
items.body:
`Task.markCompleted` starts with a guard: if the task is already completed it returns `false` immediately, before `completedAt` is assigned. So the first completion time survives. `App.completeTask` only receives that `false`, which also means "no such id", so it prints the shared message **"Task not found or already completed."**

- *"Task marked as completed." and a new time*: that branch needs `markCompleted` to return true, which it cannot do twice.
- *"Task 1 is already completed."*: no such message exists; the app cannot tell the two failure reasons apart.
- *Flips back to incomplete*: there is no code path that sets `completed` to false or clears `completedAt`.

excerpts.quote: System.out.println("Task not found or already completed.");

items.title: Why C gets id 3 in the same session
items.body:
During a session `nextId` changes in one place only: `addTask` uses it and then runs `nextId++`. After A and B it is 3. `deleteTask` finds the task, removes it from the list and returns; it never reads or writes `nextId`. So C gets **id 3**, and running the app prints "Task added with id 3."

- *deleteTask recalculates nextId*: the recalculation lives in `loadTasks`, which only runs at startup.
- *addTask reuses the lowest free id*: `addTask` takes `nextId` as it is; there is no search for gaps.
- *Deleting renumbers the other tasks*: ids are `final` fields of `Task`; nothing can change them after creation.

items.title: Why the task is saved when input runs out
items.body:
When the input stream ends, the next `scanner.nextLine()` throws `NoSuchElementException`. `run()` has no `catch` for it, but the loop sits inside `try { ... } finally { ... }`, and a `finally` block runs on every way out of the `try`, including an exception. So `saveTasksToDisk` writes the new task, and only then does the exception end the program with a stack trace.

- *Only option 5 saves*: option 5 just sets `running = false`; the save itself lives in `finally`.
- *The exception exits before any save*: that would be true without `finally`, which is the point of using it.
- *The app catches it and shows the menu*: there is no catch; the program stops after the save.

items.title: Why tasks are listed in id order after loading
items.body:
`TaskManager.loadTasks` clears the list, adds the loaded tasks in file order, and then sorts the list with `Comparator.comparingInt(Task::getId)`. `listTasks` prints `getAllTasks()` in list order. So **id 2 is listed first**, whatever order the file had.

- *File order*: that is the order before the sort, which happens on every load.
- *Newest createdAt first*: no code compares timestamps.
- *Completed tasks first*: the listing never groups by state; the [X] and [ ] marks are only drawn per line.

New tasks are appended with ever-higher ids, so within a session the list stays in id order too.

items.title: Why D gets id 3 after a restart
items.body:
At startup `TaskManager.loadTasks` replaces the list with the loaded tasks and then calls `calculateNextId`, which finds the highest id among the tasks it was given and adds one. C was deleted and the file saved without it, so the survivors are 1 and 2, and D gets **id 3**. The deleted id is handed out again; the onboarding checklist reproduces exactly this.

- *Id 4, stored in tasks.txt*: `saveTasks` writes six fields per task and no counter, so nothing remembers that 3 was used.
- *Id 1 after a restart*: the constructor sets `nextId` to 1, but `loadTasks` recalculates it from the loaded tasks right away.
- *Id 4 from a list of deleted ids*: no such list exists anywhere in the code.

items.title: Why a missing file is a normal start, not an error
items.body:
`loadTasks` checks `Files.exists(filePath)` first and returns an empty list when the file is absent. No exception is thrown, so `loadTasksFromDisk` takes the normal path and prints **"Loaded 0 task(s)."**, then the menu appears. The file is created later, when the app saves.

- *"Could not load tasks..."*: that message is only printed in the `catch` for an `IOException`.
- *An error and exit*: a missing file is handled before any reading starts.
- *"No tasks found." and an empty file*: that message belongs to option 2 when the list is empty, and nothing writes the file at startup.

items.title: How a completed task without a time is displayed
items.body:
`formatTaskForDisplay` picks the checkbox from `isCompleted()` alone, so the task shows **[X]**. The Created line is always added. The Completed line is guarded by `task.isCompleted() && task.getCompletedAt() != null`, so with an empty `completedAt` it is skipped and `formatDate` is never called with null.

- *[ ] because there is no time*: the checkbox ignores `completedAt`.
- *A Completed line copying the created time*: nothing substitutes another date; the line is simply left out.
- *It crashes*: the null check sits before the `formatDate` call, which is why the app survives this file.
